paragraphs.heading: A hunter in the stars
paragraphs.text: Orion is a striking group of stars seen in winter from the northern hemisphere. It is one of the 88 modern constellations, and it already appeared among the 48 that the astronomer Ptolemy listed in the 2nd century AD. It takes its name from a hunter in Greek myth. Its official three-letter abbreviation is "Ori".

paragraphs.heading: When and where to see it
paragraphs.text: Orion shows best in the evening from January to April, which is winter in the north and summer in the south. From May to July it sits in the daytime sky, so most places cannot see it. In the tropics it passes straight overhead. In countries near the equator, such as Kenya or Ecuador, it is overhead around midnight in December.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of the figure
paragraphs.text: Its seven brightest stars make an hourglass outline. Four of them, Rigel, Betelgeuse, Bellatrix and Saiph, mark a rough rectangle. In its middle sit the three stars of the Belt: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. A shorter line of three hangs below the Belt as the hunter's Sword, and its middle point is not a star at all but the Orion Nebula, which ranks among the sky's brightest nebulae.

paragraphs.heading: Two giant stars
paragraphs.text: Betelgeuse and Rigel are the two brightest stars in Orion, and both are supergiants. Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant close to the end of its life, and it forms the hunter's right shoulder. Its death is expected to bring a supernova explosion that might outshine the Moon and show in daylight, most likely within the next 100,000 years. Rigel is a blue supergiant that marks the hunter's left foot and is the seventh-brightest star in the night sky.

paragraphs.heading: A signpost to other stars
paragraphs.text: Orion is a handy guide for finding other stars. Follow the Belt's line toward the southeast and you reach Sirius; follow it northwest and you reach Aldebaran. A line east across the two shoulders points to Procyon. A line from Rigel through Betelgeuse leads to Castor and Pollux.

paragraphs.heading: Seen from Antarctica
paragraphs.text: Antarctica adds a strange twist. In its winter months the Sun stays below the horizon even at midday over much of the continent. Then the brightest stars of Orion can be seen for a few hours around local noon, low in the northern sky. In the southern summer, when Orion is normally a night sight, Antarctica misses it, because south of the Antarctic Circle the Sun stays up all day in that season.
